getReady.camera.title: What the camera is for
getReady.camera.checks: During the exam the camera checks only that you are there, on your own, and looking at the screen. It works on this device: no video or picture of you is recorded or sent.
getReady.camera.never: The camera never grades you and never decides anything. Anything it notices is a low-confidence note for a person to read, never an automatic result.
getReady.eyes.title: About eye contact
getReady.eyes.look: While the examiner asks and while you answer, look at her as you would on a video call.
getReady.eyes.thinkingOk: Looking away to think is completely normal.
getReady.eyes.thinkingWhy: Most people do it, and it often helps. You never need to stare at the screen, and nothing happens when you glance away.
getReady.eyes.reminder: Only a long look away from the screen while you are answering gets a reminder, and it is a gentle one: never a warning sound or a flashing screen.
getReady.eyes.neverGrade: Reminders never change your grade, and nothing ends your exam automatically.
getReady.eyes.off: This exam doesn't use the eye-contact check.

getReady.how.title: How Socratic questioning works
getReady.how.intro: This isn't a multiple-choice test. The examiner asks one question at a time and builds the next question from your own answer: it may ask you to clarify a word you used, give an example, test your idea against a tricky case, or point out when two of your answers seem to disagree.
getReady.science.summary: Why it works this way (the science behind it)
getReady.science.p1: This is the method Socrates used, called the elenchus: he questioned people who were sure they knew something and found that one of them "thinks he knows something when he does not" (Plato, Apology 21d). The questions only ever use what you yourself said, and they check whether your answers fit together.
getReady.science.whyTitle: Why follow-up questions show real understanding.
getReady.science.why: A single right answer can be remembered or guessed. Explaining why it is true, handling a case that doesn't fit and using the idea in a new situation is much harder without understanding it. Psychologists use the same approach to find out how people think: vary the questions, try a counter-suggestion, and never put the answer in the person's mouth (Piaget, 1929). Being asked to explain also tends to help people learn (Bisra et al., 2018), so the exam can teach you something too.
getReady.science.limitsTitle: Its limits, and what Gadfly does about them.
getReady.science.limit1: If two of your answers disagree, that shows something isn't settled yet, not which answer is wrong (Vlastos, 1983; Benson, 1995). You can fix either one; your course material and the grading rubric decide what is right.
getReady.science.limit2: Explaining out loud slows everyone down (Fox, Ericsson & Best, 2011). Pauses, "um"s, an accent and how fast you speak are not graded.
getReady.science.limit3: Speech recognition can mishear some accents and stuttered speech (Koenecke et al., 2020; Mujtaba et al., 2024). If the next question shows the examiner misheard you, say so and put it again in your own words.
getReady.science.limit4: One exam can't measure everything, and AI graders make mistakes (van der Vleuten et al., 2010; Zheng et al., 2023). Several AI models score each topic separately, a human examiner grades too, and a person approves your result before you see it.
getReady.science.limit5: A webcam can't tell reading from thinking (Papoutsaki et al., 2016), and voice measures can't detect stress or lying (Harnsberger et al., 2009). Camera notes and the comparison of your voice with your first answers are shown to a reviewer only as low-confidence notes, never as a verdict and never as part of your grade. The voice comparison can lead the examiner to ask an extra follow-up question.
getReady.science.refs: Full references and how each was checked: "The science behind Gadfly" in Gadfly's documentation (docs/SCIENCE.md).
getReady.rules.typed: The examiner talks to you and asks each question out loud. Your instructor has given you an accommodation: you type your answers instead of speaking them, and your microphone isn't used. Your camera must stay on for the whole exam, and the eye-contact check applies as for everyone (unless you also have the eye-contact accommodation). If the camera stops working, the exam pauses until you bring it back.
getReady.rules.typedOwnWords: Type in your own words. Pasting text into the answer box is noted for your instructor to review.
getReady.rules.spoken: The exam is spoken. The examiner talks to you and you answer out loud. Typing your answers is only possible as an accommodation your instructor grants (for a documented speech, hearing or anxiety need); ask them if you need it. Your microphone and camera must stay on for the whole exam. If either stops working, the exam pauses until you bring it back.
getReady.rules.clock: Your time starts when the examiner asks the first question, not when you press Begin exam.
getReady.rules.ownWords: Answer in your own words. Short, honest answers are better than long copied ones.
getReady.rules.dontKnow: If you genuinely don't know, say so or press I don't know. Admitting it is a real answer, not a failure, and the examiner moves on.
getReady.rules.reload: The clock is kept on the server; if you reload the page, you return to the same question.
getReady.rules.scores: You won't see scores during the exam. Your result is published once it has been graded and approved.
getReady.try.title: Try one (practice, not recorded)
getReady.try.question: Practice: in your own words, what is a habit?
getReady.try.typedHint: Type an answer in a sentence or two, then press the button. Nothing is recorded.
getReady.try.spokenHint: Answer out loud in a sentence or two, then press the button. Nothing is recorded.
getReady.try.waitMic: The button turns on once the system check above has heard your microphone.
getReady.try.followUp: Can you think of something that fits your description, but that you wouldn't call a habit?
getReady.try.followUpWhy: That's a counterexample move: the examiner tests your definition against a case built from your own words. In the real exam the follow-ups are written live from what you say.
getReady.try.dontKnowFollowUp: That's fine. Let's come at it from another side: can you name one thing you do almost every day without thinking about it?
getReady.try.dontKnowWhy: "I don't know" is an honest answer. The examiner records it and either tries an easier angle or moves on to the next topic.

getReady.language.title: Your languages
getReady.language.why: We ask so the examiner can be fair to students taking the exam in a language that isn't their first. Your answers are never used to grade you, and nothing about where you come from is ever worked out from them.
getReady.language.primary: Which language do you speak best?
getReady.language.editable: Your answers are saved when you begin and filled in for you next time; you can change them here before any exam.
